utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom, especially to you, Mr. Vanderpuye. We haven't seen you for a long time. Mr. Tolimir, we are in the middle of the cross-examination of witness Ewa Tabeau. A long time ago you indicated that you will need five to six hours for your cross-examination. And we all should try to conclude the examination of the next witness today as well, if possible. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just have a bit of information for the Trial Chamber and that is we have translations uploaded for the following exhibits: P1677, we have the B/C/S translation uploaded; P2162, we have a replacement English translation for this document; and for P2265, we have an English translation; as well as for P2444; and for P2447, we have an English and B/C/S translation, the original of that document was in French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will come back to that at a later stage in order to save court time today. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to talk about two submissions based on Rule 92 quater, that the Prosecution submitted. utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We are very grateful for that, Mr. Gajic. Thank you very much. Good morning, Ms. Tabeau. Welcome back to the courtroom. It's a long time ago that you started your testimony in this trial. I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth you made at the beginning of your testimony still applies. Mr. Tolimir is continuing his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May God's peace reign in this courtroom and may His will be done in these proceedings and not necessarily mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to greet Ms. Ewa Tabeau. I wish her a pleasant stay in this courtroom. I still have a few questions left which is neither here nor there. What matters is that we have managed to provide time for your testimony. Ms. Tabeau, can we please look at 1D949 in the e-court. Thank you. I apologise, I have not seen Mr. Vanderpuye a long time and I forgot to greet him, as well as all the others in the courtroom. We see this document which is not very legible, but this was a document which was issued by the Ministry of Labour, Social Policy, and Refugees --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, could this be enlarged a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please wait a moment. Perhaps it's only necessary to have one of the documents on the screen. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will repeat. You probably now see it better. The document was issued by the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, from the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, from its Tuzla canton. It was compiled on the 28th of July, 1995. The title of the document is: "Breakdown of Refugees from Srebrenica Accommodated in Municipalities in the Tuzla/Podrinje canton on the 28th of July, 1995." In this document it is listed that on the 20th of July, 1995, a total of 27.130 individuals were accommodated in various municipalities. And the remark reads: "In the above figures, persons accommodated at Dubrava airport are not included." And this implies those that were accommodated within the perimeter of the airport. My question to you, Ms. Tabeau, is this: Did you have an occasion to see this document and similar documents that speak about the time when the refugees from Srebrenica were accounted for? And can you tell me whether such documents have been included into your analysis? Did you include them and did you try to check those documents against any others that were compiled in the course of 1995? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the benefit of the witness, I think we should have only the English translation on the screen and be enlarged. Thank you very much. I take it, Mr. Tolimir, that you have the B/C/S version in front of you in hard copy. Ms. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see this particular document, but sources related to the so-called refugees from Srebrenica were used in our work. We discussed these issues in the report. There is an annex -- there is annex discussing the cross-referencing of the so-called refugees from Srebrenica with our lists of missing persons from Srebrenica. The major source we used for cross-referencing is called the DDPR. The source is discussed in annex 3.5, and there is another annex discussing the methodology of cross-referencing. And there is annex 3.7 in the report in which we discuss the 1997 record of Srebrenica refugees. These records are actually coming largely from the same source. It is the registration of internal displacement during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The registration was done by local authorities. At some point UNHCR got involved in the registration processes, and the outcomes of these processes were databases. One of the them, central database on displaced persons within Bosnia and Herzegovina and refugees in this country, is called DDPR. We used it as one of the main sources on surviving population from Bosnia and cross-referenced this source and the so-called 97 refugees from Srebrenica with our list of survivors. We have not said "survivors" but "missing persons," of course. Sorry. It was my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I am Tabeau, not taboo, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tabeau. I apologise for not pronouncing your name properly. And I apologise once again. This document clearly shows that very precise numbers are given rather than just estimates. Does this point to the fact that people who had been evacuated from Srebrenica were registered as well as those that had reached the territory under the control of the BiH Army in the convoy?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the refugees -- or displaced persons, more correctly, have always been registered in conflict affected countries. It is an important group of people who need protection and aid and records of displacement is an important one, so I never questioned the fact that this kind of registration was done and was done systematically. So I never questioned it in my report or any testimonies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tabeau. Do you agree with me if I say that the basic data on the number of refugees and displaced persons from Srebrenica should be the base for all the other analyses and estimates, and I am talking about the expert reports provided by demographers and similar experts? Do you also agree that your analysis should give those numbers in a separate tables, that they should not be included with all the other data? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I not only agree with you that separate analysis should be made with regard to displacement and refugees of a conflict, but I, with my people, have done several such reports which were submitted in several cases in ICTY. But here in this case, we are speaking about a different kind of report. The report we submitted is about victims, and in addition it is a particular group of victims. It is the missing persons; a very special group. We know very little in the beginning of our process about the fate of these persons. So I don't see in what way other than what we did in our work we could use data on displacement and refugees to draw conclusions about missing persons. What we did, we cross-referenced records of survivors, it would be displaced persons, refugees, non-displaced population, with records of missing persons, in order to eliminate potential survivors in the records of missing persons. That is all we did, and this is all that should and can be done when preparing a report on victims. Other than that, displacement information, refugees information, cannot be used directly to draw conclusions about victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tabeau. Please, I would like you to look at 1D949. Thank you. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to tender that document, and I would like to call up 1D947. The numbers are similar which made me make that mistake. Once again, I would like to tender 1D949 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, that is the correct number, and we have error on page 3, line 11, there is a different number which is incorrect. The document will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 1D949 shall be assigned Exhibit D313. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we would like to have 1D947 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see the document on the screen. It is again not very legible. Can it be -- yes, thank you. This is a document issued by UNPROFOR. It's Sector North-east whose headquarters were in the Tuzla air base. The document was issued on the 4th of August, 1995. The document reads: "Subject: Srebrenica, displaced persons situation update." The following points are made as an update to the current humanitarian situation in SNE concerning the Srebrenica displaced persons. "Total number: 35.632 (approximately). "Housed in private accomodation: 17.383. "Housed in collective centres: 9.749. "Tuzla air base camp: 6.500." This is a supplement to the first table which indicated 27.000 people with the 6.500 who were at the base. During your work, did you have available to you the update that UNPROFOR had concerning people who fled from Srebrenica to the territory under the control of the BiH and to the Tuzla air base camp? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have this particular document, but the number as such doesn't come to me as a surprise, the 35.600 something. If you, sir, refer to annex 3.7, then you will find some statistics that are quite comparable to this number. In my estimation, it would be about 30.000 displaced persons from Srebrenica in more or less the same period. As you see from our report, we cross-referenced these records with the records of missing persons. We identified about 100 individuals potentially overlapping between missing persons and displaced persons. We clarified these cases with the authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and compared with additional sources we have in our office, that would be ICMP identifications of victims, and found many matches among the identified for our potential 100 survivors. And the conclusion is that is not correct to believe that these 100 potential candidates are the persons reported as missing on our list. So the exercise ended with the conclusion that no record of a missing person should be removed from the list as a reported survivor, displaced person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tabeau. Under C in the document it says that: "Plan for movement of displaced persons population from Tuzla air base to collective centres is co-ordinated with BiH civil defence staff through and by UNHCR head of office. Displaced persons will be transported with BiH transport and moved to accommodations which have been repaired or renovated by either SEA, IRC," and so on and so forth. Please, did you establish the final list once those people from the air base were transported to accomodation centres that had been repaired or renovated by representatives of various international organisations? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need to work with these kinds of lists because the sources on survivors that we used for our work actually comprised these kind of developments. This particular document is dated, as far as I remember, August 1995, if we go to the -- yes. We worked with 1997 records, compiled by the authorities in Tuzla and later in Sarajevo in the Ministry For Displaced Persons and Refugees, and we also used the 2000 version of the DDPR, that is the central system registering displaced persons and refugees, and we as well used other sources on survivors; that is, the sources that would be reporting on both displaced persons and non-displaced persons. That would be the three large voter's registers that we used to search for survivors. I think that this is quite some work meant to find any possible survivors, and it must be remembered that these searches were run in the context of this one particular group: Missing persons, the persons of whom no record existed as to their fate after the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, Mrs. Tabeau, could you tell me, since you studied all this, whose data is more precise: Those that were based on the lists of displaced persons and refugees in accomodation centres or the data from 1997? Did you cross-reference those two sets of data in order to establish any discrepancies?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the 1997 data with the 1995 data, if I may clarify; right? Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, the 1995 data and the 1997 data. Did you cross-reference those two sets of data as you have already indicated in your previous answer? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, as a matter of fact, didn't have to cross-reference anything in this particular case because the records of 1997 refugees discussed in annex 3.7 largely come from the local authorities in Tuzla, who actually registered the displacement from Srebrenica in the period to which this document is referring. So actually I have the data to work with and that would be the 1997 records of Srebrenica refugees. As you will see in this annex, there were four CDs [Realtime transcript read in error "cities"] that were submitted to the Office of the Prosecutor. The CDs one to three were coming directly from Tuzla authorities, and only one CD was coming from the Ministry for Displaced Persons and Refugees in Sarajevo. So these three CDs jointly comprised about 20.000 records of displaced persons, so I simply had this data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The record should be record. We are not talking about "cities" but "CDs." Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tabeau. Please, since you said in the first and second parts of your answer that you relied on documents from 1997, my question is: Are the documents from 1997 more valid, more relevant, than the documents that were developed in 1995 after people left collection centres?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the 1997 records shouldn't be seen as made in 1997. These are records that were collected over a longer period of time starting already during the war, in this case 1995, and later, and the record is dated as of 1997; that means, it is the status of this data of this registration system that goes back to all the information that was obtained in the course of time. So it is not about what is more reliable, 1995 or 1997, it is just the data coming from a dynamic system that is systematically updated as the new data is coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tabeau. Was it finally documented definitively, everyone that came out with the military column and the civilians, was it supposed to be identical, this new data from 1997? Was it identical to the records of collection centres from 1995?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you are referring to a column. I refer -- I will refer to records of displaced persons often also called, incorrectly, refugees in this context, so it is just the population who ended in the Tuzla region as displaced people; that is, people who no more were living in their homes. Was it identical with this 1995 information? This is all we have, and knowing how the data was collected I can say this is the same information as was subsequently obtained or produced by the authorities from Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D947 is a document I would like to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D947 shall be assigned Exhibit D314. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Please, could we now display 1D958. That is a report from the World Health Organization on persons displaced from Srebrenica to the Tuzla/Podrinje canton. The document also identifies the number of displaced persons on 29 July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And it says -- can you see it now so we can all follow?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's not on the screen. Did you provide us with a correct number? The document with that number is not listed in your list of documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My mistake. It should be 948. I should have followed the same order as before. 1D948 follows 1D947. I apologise to the electronic courtroom and Ms. Tabeau. We need, in fact, 1D948. It's a report on recently displaced people from Srebrenica to Tuzla-Podrinje canton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: They say the total is 34.341. In private accomodation, 17.137. In collective centres, 9.804 persons. And at the air base, 7.400. My question is: Did you have occasion to see this document before while you were making your analysis and your expert report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. As this document is not really a source for me in my analysis of missing persons and exhumed persons and identified persons. So I, myself, have estimated and presented in several reports. The displacement from Srebrenica was very, very considerable, especially with regard to the Muslim population living in Srebrenica area and neighbouring municipalities. Many of them ended in the Tuzla canton, so this is yet another confirmation that the statement about the large-scale displacement from Srebrenica is correct, but it is not helpful to use this kind of statement in the analysis of missing persons, of mass graves and identified people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tabeau. And is it useful to have a document like this when considering the number of displaced persons from Srebrenica to the Tuzla-Podrinje canton?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is better to work with records of displaced persons and refugees, and these records exist and are much more correct than these kind of rough statistics. So it is just one of contextual documents that confirm the scale of displacement, no more than that. But statistically speaking, I would always prefer to work with individual records of victims, displaced persons, refugees, killed persons, missing persons, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tabeau. My question is: For demographers, are numbers on the population and movement more interesting? Is this the kind of data that indicates where these people are accommodated and in what numbers?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it indicates the places where people were accommodated and some numbers, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like this document, 1D948, to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D948 shall be assigned Exhibit D315. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank the Registrar. Could e-court please display P1777. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That is a list from the OTP on missing persons from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we need page 91 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we are looking for that page, would you kindly tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, would you tell us, please, were you involved in the drafting of this OTP list?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we then look at the name -- I don't know how to deal with this, because maybe all of the names are protected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's very easy. We can go into private session for that part of your examination. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence has tried to facilitate the proceedings by preparing hard copies of the document so we don't have to call it up in e-court every time. If the usher could just distribute the list to everyone in the courtroom, to all the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please, that's helpful. Especially for the witness. Mr. Tolimir, are you going to mention specific names on the list? In that case, we should go into private session, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have now distributed the document, so I don't have to mention any names.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I would like to ask Ms. Tabeau to look at entry number 7. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if you could answer this question: Does it follow from this that the person under number 7 was born on the 2nd of May and went missing on the 14th of July, 1995, in a place called Buljim-Bratunac (redacted) (redacted) Thank you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't follow. On the first page, I am now dealing with page number 91, which is on the screen. Then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Record number seven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, then that is the next page. Yes, thank you. It's clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I emphasize that the date of birth is 2nd May 1952 and the date when the person went missing is 1995, 14 July.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 1D950 [Realtime transcript read in error "1D590"].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. There is an error in the record. It's 1D950.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That is the number which was interpreted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. What we see here is a decision by the lower court in Lukavica determining that the death of the person under number 7 occurred on the 7th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And the statement of reasons indicates the cause of death. Since there is no translation I have to read it to you. I will leave out only the name and surname, and I will be referring to the person as entry 7. The proponent, I will leave out the name, submitted an application to this court to prove the death of her spouse, leaving out the name, stating that as a member of the 28th Mounted Battalion he was killed on 7 July 1995 on an elevation called Ljubisavici. The claims from the application of the proponent have been confirmed by witnesses Muhudin Hasanovic [phoen] and Mevlida Osmanovic as well as the temporary holder of custody, Osman Omerovic. The aforenamed persons stated that, leaving out the name, was during the war a member of the 28th Mountain Battalion, and his unit mounted an attack on the enemy elevation called Ljubisavici on 7 July 1995. The name of the elevation is Ljubisavici, on which occasion entry number 7 was killed. [As read] "The next day on the 8th of July 1995 he was buried at the town cemetery called Kazani. These facts follow from the death certificate 07/02-216-22/50, issued by the command of the 28th Division on 19 March 1997 which states that entry number 7 was killed on 7 July 1995 at the Ljubisavici elevation." I will not read the passage which follows which states that it was published in the Official Gazette, et cetera. Now, based on this, Ms. Tabeau, I would like to ask: In this case, the case of the person under number 7, is it an obvious discrepancy between the list of the OTP which states that the person went missing on the 14th of July whereas this court decision indicates that he was killed on 7th July 1995?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, nothing is obvious. First of all, it is very good to ask what kind of document is this. It is a court declaration of a person death. The declaration is issued in response to a request from a family member of this person. The family member -- the family reported this person as missing. They don't have information about what happened to him. If they did know what happened to this person, there wouldn't be necessary to have a court to decide -- to declare this person dead. So these kind of declarations were issued for the missing persons, conditionally on the fulfillment of a number of requirements. The same type of declarations were used for the list of 58 names that General Tolimir addressed at some point earlier and which I studied in order to make an assessment of the possibility whether these cases were of people who died in different circumstances and different places at different moments of time than what is claimed in the OTP lists of missing persons. These court declarations, as a matter of fact, usually don't -- are not based on precise information about the death, because the death is actually something that needs to be declared as the person is missing. So the circumstances, the date, the place, the cause of death, are unknown. This particular case, based on witness statements, based on what they were tell the court, seems to be more complete in the sense that the witnesses told the court about what happened. And based on what they said, the court issued a decision. At the same time, in the OTP list, this person is reported as a missing, with the date of disappearance 14th of July (redacted)

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, it's a very difficult question. As a matter of fact, what I would do in such case, I would go back and check both sources because they contradict each other in some sense. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: So what I would do is I would go and check all the details and come back with a conclusion. In both cases much more information should be available. The ICMP will most certainly have complete reports from the family members of the person. It is easy to figure out who reported the person to the ICMP. Is this the same -- exactly same person reported in both the court declaration and in the ICMP record, et cetera, et cetera. So these kind of cases, at first impression contradictory, and with a serious question which source should be trusted, can be sorted out rather easily. This is what I have done for the 58 names addressed earlier by General Tolimir, and the same can be done with this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tabeau. Now, please, several facts are stated here that we need to bear in mind: One, that the 28th Division issued a certificate on 19 March, 1997, that the person was killed in combat on the 7th of July, that's one; and second, two witnesses - I won't mention their names again - say that he was buried at the local cemetery called Kazani, and the wife claims the same. And the court determined it based on witness statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: (redacted) And could the same family claim him as gone missing from the column, as saying that he was killed earlier while being a member of the column, as determined by the court? What should be more reliable to General Tolimir, a court determination or an assessment made based on an analysis?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell General Tolimir what he should decide because it is his decision, but what I would do, as I said, I would study this particular document in a broader context of all available information related to this case. And this is what I did, and if you give me a second I will check my records because I possibly have more information right now in the court, or I will do it in the break, but things are sometimes not as straightforward as they look. For instance, the same names can be associated with a totally different person, and there might be a very small difference in the date of birth, small but significant in the sense that this would be two different persons. These kind of things happen quite often, and this is why we, in our method, don't work with single source and single document, we work with a number of sources, related sources, that overlap in the sense that one given case can be compared across the sources. And what we would do, we would go back first to the 1991 census record and check how many people with these same names or very similar names were reported there in the census, and we would track their fates in other sources of information. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted) We would go to other databases. If this person is a known death, as it seems according to this court declaration, the case should be reported in official death notifications, compiled by statistical authorities in both entities in the federation and Republika Srpska, and we have these records in our office. We would search for the person, compare the records, we would check all kinds of sources. And only then would we draw a conclusion. So I can do this. I am not sure then how Tolimir can do this, but I can help, I can assist this Court to clarify these kind of cases, and this is actually what we have been doing since the very beginning of our work on Srebrenica. Srebrenica is a mass atrocity case. It is very -- it would be very difficult to analyse all the cases, one by one, approximately 8.000 victims. To clarify what happened to them by questioning witnesses is actually an impossible thing to do. So what instead can be done, there exists lists of victims issued by reliable organs, and we use these lists, cross-reference them, and come up with our findings. This is, I think, the best approach to answer these discrepancies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, I would like to put an additional question to you in relation to that. Thank you for this explanation. Earlier in one of your answers you said: "It could be sorted out quite easily. This is what I have done for the 58 names addressed earlier by General Tolimir." Are you referring to the beginning of your cross-examination in this trial where we dealt with similar cases, and did you do this research in the time between when after the last day in court in this trial? What was the result of this check for the 58 names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is, indeed, so that the 58 names I mentioned came up earlier this year. I think, already, for the first time during the testimony of Helge Brunborg, as far as I'm not wrong. And the claim of the Defence is that there are 58 persons listed on the OTP lists of missing persons that, as a matter of fact, died at different places, at different dates than the fall of Srebrenica, and in addition they died of natural causes of death and shouldn't be kept on the OTP list. So I studied these particular 58 names recently and made a little report about my findings. All these 58 names were taken from a book by Milivoje Ivanisevic. So that's the actual source for this the names. All of these names were listed by him based on these kind of court declarations as the one we are having on our screen. These declarations were issued by local courts in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Most of them rather in distant past from now, so in the year, say, 1997, 1998, something like that, and all these declarations were addressed to the courts by the families because the families actually didn't know what happened to their relatives. As a matter of fact, these declarations I studied were issued in the context of missing persons. As -- the conclusion -- I did two things: First of all, I collected the actual declarations and studied them myself to confirm whether, indeed, these declarations related to unrelated cases, not Srebrenica victims, and the second part of the work was in line with what I just mentioned, it was cross-referencing of these names with the sources the OTP has -- I have in my unit, including the 1991 population census, the missing persons list, the ICMP identification of these persons. To keep it brief, in both cases, I didn't find any reasons to consider any of these persons unrelated to the fall of Srebrenica. As a matter of fact, there is a lot of evidence to the contrary. Many of these individuals were identified by ICMP. Only, I think, as far as I remember, one wasn't, and three actually were siblings' identifications, but the rest were identifications that link these names to certain mass graves and records of DNA identification. So all in all -- actually, two records, as far as I remember, were reported in the court declarations as deaths from 1992, but I checked that these two names were actually different persons than the persons included in the OTP lists. Those that were on the OTP lists were with very similar or even identical names, slight differences in dates of births but were different persons and died in the fall of Srebrenica. The 1992 records on the Ivanisevic list were, as a matter of fact, different people who died in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just one brief additional question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you didn't have any reason to change your findings in your previous report; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you -- as you said, you compiled these findings, the research in relation to these 58 persons in a little report --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- given to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the report should have been disclosed to everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was -- that would be my question to Mr. Vanderpuye, if that report was disclosed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Indeed it was, Mr. President, and it's uploaded as 65 ter 7518, which I intended to introduce it and to use it in a redirect which, obviously, will be much briefer now. But the Defence does have the report. I do note, though, that I don't believe the report has been translated as yet. A request was submitted but it's not completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this update. Mr. Tolimir, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. My legal assistant wants to say something about the documents that Ms. Tabeau has just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, yesterday we reviewed documents. Before we had not had an occasion to see over a hundred pages of documents similar to the one on the screen. We could not read them on the electronic disclosure system. Of course, we managed to review a lot of those pages, but not all. We hope that we will continue dealing with these documents. Unfortunately, there is still no translation of the document into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could D950 be admitted into evidence, 1D950. This is the document dealing with the person who was buried in the local graveyard before the conflict in Srebrenica and subsequently in -- his body was excavated from a mass grave. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D950 shall be assigned Exhibit D316, marked for identification, pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now look at P1777. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a Prosecutor's list of people missing from Srebrenica. It was compiled in 2009. I don't think it should be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are interested in page 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since we can't say the names, we are interested in entry number five from the top of the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We can see the names. The names are on the screen. We can see them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we can. But I am not going to read them. Everybody can see the names. I am interested in number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, does it arise from this that the person under number 5 was born on the 21st of January 1995 and that the last time he was seen in Potocari on the 13th of July, 1995, in Potocari. And that his death was confirmed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The date of birth in this list is 21st of January 1965, not 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, with this correction, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I agree with Mr. President. I misspoke. 21st of January, 1996 -- or, rather, 1965. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, was it confirmed that the last time he was seen was in Potocari and then that he was confirmed dead?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what we see on this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to show the witness 1D951. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now we can see a decision where it says that the person under number 5 was born on the 20th of January in Srebrenica and that his family had filed a request for the date of death to be confirmed as the 15th March in Zepa municipality of Rogatica. 15th of March, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we go to page 3 in e-court? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, we can see another document issued by the municipal court in Kladanj. This is a decision to correct the previous decision of the same court in Kladanj, and in this decision it says that the date of birth would be deleted and that it would be replaced by another date of birth which would be the 21st of January, 1965. Everything else remains the same as before. The decision that we see contains a correction of the date of birth of the person who died and whose name is listed under number 5. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now go back to 1D951, page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now we can see it. This is a decision pursuant to which number 5 was declared dead, and at 15th of March 1995 is hereby determined as the date of death. And I am going to read from the statement of reasons where it says: "Based on the testimonies of the applicant and witnesses, the court has established that" - person under number 5, whose name I am not going to read - "went missing on the 15th of March, 1995," as it stays says here, but this is an error -- no, it's not an error, "he went missing on the 15th of March, 1995, as a member of the Army of BiH, and he went missing in Zepa. From then on there have been no news of his life or death." My question is this: Does this decision clearly point to the fact that the court had to establish the date of birth twice? You also mentioned such instances that were aimed at avoiding manipulations. Does it also clearly show that person under number 5 who died in circumstances unrelated to the events surrounding the month of July 1995? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you're asking whether the date of birth has been established twice, obviously it was, and probably because a reliable document in which the date of birth would be reported was unavailable or became available at a later moment of time. Inconsistencies in dates of birth are seen very often across various documents reporting on the same persons, especially if information is coming based on witness statements or just statements. People are very bad in remembering dates. So the second part of your question was -- I think there wasn't second part, so it was the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see here that the date of death was the 15th of March, which was a few months before the date indicated in the report -- in the Prosecutor's report, and that the place of death was Zepa and not Srebrenica? Thank you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's not forget that this court declaration is about a missing person, a person whose fate is unknown. So we can't speak about the actual date of death, the actual place of death, the actual cause of death. Why? Because there is no proof other than statements of some people who are saying things they are saying. The date 15th of March is the date of last seen. This is when the person was last seen by those who appeared before the court to give their statement, and they are saying they saw the person in Zepa. That's it. This is all the document is telling us. In order to be sure that this was the case with this person, a lot of additional work is required. In our records, ICRC records, coming also from informants, close relatives, there is a different date of last seen. The date is the 13th of July, and the place is different. Whom to trust more and better, this is a very good question. What we believe is the right thing to do, it is important to cross-reference these kind of statements with the DNA record of identification of such people. For many of these kind of cases, such identifications are available. For some, not yet. But because these persons are often included in siblings' identifications, this is a sign for us this information is coming. For some other cases there won't be information other than the report about the missing, the disappearance of this person. If I am asked which source I trust more when it comes to reporting of disappearances, missing persons, I do trust the ICRC. Why? Because it is an organisation that has been collecting information about missing persons for a very long time. They have developed procedures, approaches, how to do it right. They, for instance, use questionnaires, structured questionnaires in which information is collected about not only just names and date of disappearance. There is much more in there, in these questionnaires. There is also some information about the informants, and we know that ICRC does not accept information from anybody. They require that the informant is a close relative. They check the ID of the informant. So they have an interview. They speak about what happened. And it is all available from the questionnaires. The other informant, I don't know. I have no idea who are those people. Perhaps they are relatives of the wife who went to court and requested that a declaration would be issued. Why did she need a declaration? Perhaps because of property. I don't know why. Perhaps because of some other things. So in order to have a clear idea about the quality of these statements, I would have to go back and contact these people and talk to them and check whether what this statement is telling us is actually the truth. So it is not a quick decision to decide what -- who is right, this court declaration or ICRC or ICMP. It is a process, it is an investigation, and in many cases this investigation can be done here using statistical databases. But in some other cases even this is not enough. In some cases it is necessary to go back and find these witnesses and to talk to them, as OTP often does, and this is the way to make sure that the information provided to this Court is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Tabeau. Now, please tell us, the applicant in this case, isn't she the closest relative to the missing person? She was his wife. And did the court use her testimony and the testimony of witnesses in order to establish that he went missing on the 15th of March, 1995, as an army member in Zepa? And in this courtroom, should we have the records of all the courts, all the decisions of all the courts showing what they based their decisions on? Should I, as an accused, trust the decisions of such courts or should we go through the exercise of reestablishing the data?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think the witness answered this question already in detail and explained the whole procedure she and her colleagues were following to establish if such a declaration gives reason to change the previous findings. She explained in detail and at length how, in her opinion, it would be the best way to check the information.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In that case, if we apply the same parameter to all court decisions, I have no other questions for this witness. This brings my cross-examination to an end. I just wanted to present different cases that were treated differently. I did not want to apply the same criteria to every missing person. And finally, I would like to tender this document into evidence, 1D951. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This document will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D951 shall be assigned Exhibit D317, marked for identification, pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, and to clarify the situation, my comment was in relation to your last question. Nothing else. Because you asked for the best way to establish the truth and that was just the last answer of the witness, in principle. Nevertheless, I take it that this concludes your cross-examination. We must have our first break now and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, you have the floor for your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And good morning to you, Your Honours. I haven't had a chance to greet everyone, so good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And good morning to you, Dr. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have a relatively few number of questions to ask you, so let me get started. You were asked some questions based on a few documents that General Tolimir put to you. I have them as 1D949, and this related to a document that presented certain figures, it's D313, presented certain figures concerning refugees or displaced persons related to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is now D313.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you were also presented with another document, 1D947, which is D314; and 948, which is D315. All of these documents presented figures of people that were displaced or referred to as refugees concerning the Srebrenica events. You indicated during the course of your cross-examination that this was distinct from the -- you wrote your report concerning missing persons. So what I would like to ask is if you could perhaps clarify for us and for Chamber what the distinction is between those types of records and the report that you produced concerning missing persons, are they related to one another, are they distinct from one another? If you could explain that.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already mentioned this earlier during my cross-examination that records of missing persons and records of displaced persons are two different types of records. Displaced persons are, obviously, survivors who are registered because of the fact they lost their homes and don't have a place to live in. Missing persons is a separate category. These are people who are believed they didn't survive the conflict, and this belief is not just a belief based on nothing. It is based on evidence from exhumation and identification projects of victims from mass graves. There is an extremely significant overlap between identified persons and exhumation records and records of missing persons. That's the foundation of this belief. So when it comes to analysis, records of displaced persons, of course, obviously are unrelated to those of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Just a follow-up on your immediate answer. You say, "displaced persons are unrelated to those of missing persons." Are there any circumstances, tell me if you can, where a displaced person can also be a missing person? To me, it's -- to me, a layperson, it's one and the same thing. A displaced person can present themselves as missing as well. Is that possible in your area of expertise? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that it is not, in fact, possible for a displaced person to be a missing person at the same time, because a missing person is somebody whose whereabouts are unknown and for a long, long time. So that's the reason that the person is registered as a missing person. When it comes to displacement, we have records, incomplete, deficient, but we do have records. So these people that physically exist can be contacted, can be spoken to, so that's a totally different group. I hope it clarifies.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I may just ask you a follow-up question to Her Honour's question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please, Judge Nyambe has a follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes. If we can put it the other way around, can a missing person turn up as a displaced person at some point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only if there is a misreporting of some kind. It happens that families include missing persons among the displaced of their families, but these are incidental instances that are absolutely marginal and insignificant. But, yeah, that the missing person after a while would appear as a displaced person, yeah, in theory it might be so, but I am thinking of people who left the country, move overseas, and don't show any sign of life. But -- even the family doesn't know and believe -- the family believes it is a missing person, but again I wouldn't think this is a massive process. These are, yeah, infrequent incidents, I would say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just have two follow-up questions to that. The first is: In the figures that we have seen that General Tolimir presented to you in D313, I think, or 315, is it your understanding that the numbers that we see there, roughly 34.000 or 35.000 people displaced or refugees in respect of the Srebrenica event, that those numbers include or do not include people that are missing as is reported in your -- in your analysis?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: These figures on displaced persons do not include missing persons. That is what we checked by cross-referencing relevant sources of information, and at several occasions we did so, and the persons that were marked as potential survivors out of this exercise were just 12 people, and they are listed in our report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And, formally speaking, as a demographer, in your analysis of -- in your experience, rather, in analysing a multitude of records regarding displaced persons and missing persons, is it formally generally documented or an expectation that displaced persons are people that whose whereabouts are known that can be accounted for as distinguished from missing persons or is the line somewhat blurred, professionally speaking?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think the line is blurred. These two groups are clearly distinguished in the way how they are recorded and presented in all kinds of circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I'd just like to move to another area, and that is your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 7518 in e-court, please. Just so the record is clear, this relates to the report on 58 Srebrenica cases that was raised by the Defence during the course of the cross-examination. Mr. President, I would have to move to add this to the 65 ter exhibit list because it wasn't originally on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, do you have any objection to add this document to the 65 ter exhibit list?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have no objection, except that the Prosecutor could have tendered the document we have had admitted during our cross-examination in this segment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I am not sure if I understand your comment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. My comment was that the document should be identical to the document we used in the first part of our cross-examination. That's all, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it that this is the report we discussed earlier during the cross-examination when I asked Ms. Tabeau if there is a report about these 58 cases. This is the report. And you said you have no objection to add it to the 65 ter exhibit list. Leave is granted to do that, Mr. Vanderpuye. Now Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes, just a follow-up question to understand the difference between "missing person" and "displaced person." My understanding of a displaced person during war times is one who has been displaced by the war and moves from his usual place of abode to another place, and then is registered. At that point they become a displaced person; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Okay. Now what happened to this individual before they are registered as displaced persons? To their families, they are missing persons, no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is what happens between the registration and the moment a person goes missing or disappears. There is a period of uncertainty because there is a hope at the family that the person would join them, and sometimes occasionally they even report, as I said, such people as displaced persons. I can't say more about it, because that is all what can happen in this period. But in this particular case, we are discussing, in this courtroom, it is not that the records of missing persons we have used for our work were taken in this uncertain period when many things were happening, displacement and killings and combat activities, we are -- we have used for our work very many additions of the ICRC list of missing persons, starting with the 1997 edition, then 1998, 2000, 2004, 2005, the latest is 2008. So it is not that we have taken a sample dated at a given moment, an early moment in time when the war was still going on. We have confirmed these records again and again and again in order to make sure that we work with the right information. So that is the whole point of updating this work, that we wouldn't be working with records of missing persons who eventually were found alive. ICRC has identified a few cases of such people. They are explicitly flagged in ICRC records as found alive, and we separated them, excluded them from our analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: So then this process is ongoing? Potentially somebody listed as missing could turn up somewhere still alive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, theoretically, yes, but we are speaking of very small numbers. I don't remember exactly the number, but say 30 people, 50 people at most, found alive out of 22- 23.000. These are insignificant numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you what we have in e-court here. You recognise this as your report, Dr. Tabeau?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it's entitled: "Report on 58 allegedly unjustified Srebrenica cases."

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And dated 28 July, 2011?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In the introduction here you explain the reason and the purposes that you carried out this particular analysis.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And then you indicate a number of sources that you consulted in putting the report together.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you just briefly tell the Trial Chamber what those sources were? You don't have to -- you don't have to tell us what you did with them just yet, but just what they are?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On first group of sources, included the actual court declarations based on which this list was compiled. Second group of sources included the OTP sources, that would be the 1991 population census, the 2009 OTP list of missing person, and including the information about the identification, and finally we also used the latest ICMP update on Srebrenica victims of December 2010.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And were the methods that you used in order to compare the data that was provided concerning these 58 names to the material that you've identified the same or similar to the methods that you've used previously in connection with, for example, the April 2009, I believe it is, report on Srebrenica missing and dead?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The methods are the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And what I would like to do is to briefly to go into what your findings were with respect to the 58 names that you examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We will have to go to page 2 of the report for this, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you summarised them here. But I wonder if you could explain those findings a little bit more so that the Trial Chamber has a good understanding of what you did in order to reach these results. Here you say initially that some 44 cases out of 58 that were reported in these decisions. Can you tell us what that shows or what that means?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This first paragraph relates to the outcomes of cross-referencing the list of 58 names with the actual court declarations. In total, we received approximately -- not approximately, 58 documents plus 1 irrelevant that was excluded completely. The question was whether these 58 documents cover the actual individuals from the list. So it was a matter of checking what kind of documentation of the cases was received. And the conclusion is for 44 cases, we see from these documents that these persons were presented in the court declarations as missing persons; moreover, as related to the fall of Srebrenica. Further, two persons were reported in the court declarations as disappeared in 1992 and were declared as dead with dates of death in 1992, and for these two persons we later checked, these were different individuals than those that we have on our OTP lists. In addition, there were three persons in the court declarations that were different from those names on the 58 list. For nine cases there was no documentation, but generally the conclusion is that there was enough documentation to -- to see that the cases documented were not presented the way as they were communicated by the Defence to this Court as based on the book Milivoje Ivanisevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just want to make sure that we are clear on the record, when you refer to documentation in this context, are you referring to the B and H court decisions that were provided pursuant to a request made by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the documentation. This is what I understand under it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You indicate in the second paragraph under this heading that there was cross-referencing with OTP lists, and based upon that 52 cases were confirmed to be on the Srebrenica missing and identified persons list.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is in this paragraph that I discuss the results of cross-referencing the list of 58 names with the OTP sources. They matched very well, except for the fact that two persons listed with very similar, almost identical, names and similar but different dates of birth. These two indicated as deaths in 1992 in the documents are different persons on the OTP list. Generally, 52 out of 58 were confirmed as missing, OTP missing persons, and at the same time as identified persons according to the ICMP DNA identification records; 52 records, both missing and identified. Four persons were confirmed as just missing persons. For three out of four, identification is available in the form of siblings' identification. So it seems it's coming but not yet available for complete names. Only as sibling identification. And, yeah, that would be 58, so that is the conclusion from this exercise. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You testified on cross-examination that - and I think it might have been pursuant to a question that was put to you by Her Honour Judge Nyambe - that if there was -- if you were to compare the records, or if there was an inconsistency between the records that were provided and the OTP records, (redacted) (redacted) that that would be your preferred method of establishing what the fate of that person was. Do you recall saying something to that effect?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We discussed this. I think it goes -- and this is what I said, that the approach we have taken for this work is based on the ICMP confirmations. This is an important part to us. If a given missing person is or not confirmed in the DNA identification records, and it is about the reliability of both ICRC and ICMP as the record makers in each case. It goes into the mandates but also the methods they operate, the standard procedures they use, general approach how things are done.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I think I may need to correct myself, and it may have been the result of a question that was put to you by General Tolimir about that, but in particular I want to draw your attention to one document that General Tolimir showed you which concerned a person that we've referred to in the record as entry number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that was in P1777. It would have been, I think it's page 91 of that document, but we had hard copies distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This was a person who -- for whom a certificate -- or, rather, a court record was received indicating a data of death of 7 July, 1995, as you may recall?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That individual was, according to that record, ostensibly buried on the 8th, I believe, of July, in a local grave. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as we discussed earlier today I compare related sources of information, major sources being the ICRC records of missing persons and ICMP records of DNA identification. And these records jointly with the court record doesn't seem to be obvious contradiction to what was observed by some witnesses earlier this year, by March 1995. So it is perfectly possible, in my eyes, that the person disappeared in July 1995 at -- this was reported on the ICRC by some close relatives of the person, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you had mentioned that there were included in this material, that is the records that you received, some deaths that were indicated in 1992. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. We will have to go back to 65 ter 7518. And we'll need to go to page 8. And just for the benefit of General Tolimir it does read at section 2.4, it refers to the two deaths -- two 1992 deaths which are referred to in the report as case 13 and 50, and indicates how that material or those cases were analysed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And Dr. Tabeau, you can tell us a little bit about how you did that.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In table 7, there are results from my searches in the 1991 population census --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This page should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The search was done using the names. First name, father's name, and the surname of both individuals. First individual, I won't say the name of the person, is presented by showing four different records from the census. All these four individuals have identical last name, first name, father's name; the differences are seen in the date of birth. The date of birth reported in the census for each of these individual is one from 1958, one from 1962, then 1964, 1956. One -- the first one is born in 1958, the second one is born in 1956. One is from Bratunac, one is from Srebrenica. So in the actual court declaration provided to us, the individual born in 1958 is covered and in the OTP lists of missing persons and identified, the individual born in 1956 is covered. So obviously two different persons. The second case is of the same nature. The more confusing part is the date of birth. One of the individuals is found in the census and presented in the second panel of this table. One is born in 1941 and one in 1940. Again, different municipalities, and the same names. And similarly, one -- the one born in 1941 is covered in the actual court declaration and the one born in 1940 in the OTP records. So the census information actually was extremely useful, allowed me to establish how many people with the same names lived in Bosnia in the outbreak of the war and, obviously, they experienced different fates. This happens sometimes and we can see it in our lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just in conclusion: Of the 58 names that have been identified by the Defence and by Milivoje Ivanisevic in his book, how many of these names actually -- that is, you know, conflict with the list of names that are indicated in the OTP list of missing and dead related to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the list of 58 persons was presented by General Tolimir as conflicting in its entirety, so all the 58 names were suggested either to be taken off from the OTP records, but the conclusion from this study is there is no need to take off even one record from our lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Tabeau. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to note that the third annex which concerns the results of documents that have been reviewed and cross-referenced concerning these 58 names is a -- it's a spreadsheet and so we'll provide that on a CD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Tabeau --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just one correction for the record, Your Honours. 65 ter document 7518 was assigned Exhibit P2586 under seal, marked for identification pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Ms. Tabeau, you will be pleased to hear that this now concludes your examination in this trial. utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, is the next witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, you will be first examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Elderkin, and later in cross-examination by Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Elderkin, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone else in the courtroom, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And witness, good morning to you. As you know my name is Rupert Elderkin. And if there is anything that I or anyone else asks you that is unclear, then please let me know and I will do my best to rephrase the question. We start, please, by stating your full name.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Dragan Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Are you a Bosnian Serb?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday did you also read in your own language the transcript of an interview that you gave to investigators from this Tribunal in December of 2004?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And did you also read in your own language the notes of an interview that you gave to American investigators in June of 2005?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TODOROVIC
